summary: Presents application-specific routing requirements for urban low-power and lossy networks, where sensing and actuating nodes are placed outdoors in cities to improve living conditions and monitor things like environmental rules. It informs what routing protocols must support.

eli5.summary: Many tiny sensors around a city need to send readings with little power. This note lists what a routing method must handle for such networks.

subtitle: What a routing protocol must do to connect huge numbers of tiny, battery-powered sensors and actuators spread across a city.

tldr.problem: Cities are expected to fill with outdoor sensing and actuating nodes (smart meters, weather and pollution sensors, street lights) that are cheap, short on power and connected over unreliable wireless links, and ordinary routing protocols do not suit them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the network elements, typical use cases and traffic patterns, then lists IPv6 routing requirements such as scalability, parameter-constrained routing, autonomous configuration, multicast and anycast support, tolerance of network change, and acceptable latency.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document for the ROLL (Routing Over Low-Power and Lossy networks) work. It guides the design of routing protocols for urban sensor networks rather than defining one.

facts.label: Node distances
facts.value: Hundreds of meters to one kilometer

today: RFC 5548 is an Informational RFC from May 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements for routing protocols and does not define a protocol itself.

sections.title: Urban Low-Power and Lossy Networks
sections.content:
An Urban Low-Power and Lossy Network (U-LLN) is built from three kinds of wireless elements: sensors, actuators and routers. Sensors measure things such as gas, water and electricity use (smart metering), weather, pollution and allergens. Actuators control urban devices such as street or traffic lights, and there are far fewer of them than sensors. Routers close coverage and routing gaps; some also connect to wider infrastructure such as the Internet and are called LBRs (Low-Power and Lossy Network Border Routers). A device can play more than one role.

The RFC expects between 10^2 and 10^7 sensing nodes for a given application, deployed in batches of hundreds to thousands at random places within constraints such as along a road or river. Nodes are resource constrained: cheap hardware, little memory and no infinite energy source, powered by batteries, energy scavenging, passive RFID or mains. Battery shelf life is usually 10 to 15 years. Nodes may sit from several hundred meters to one kilometer apart, so not every node reaches an LBR in one hop.

Links are volatile because of wireless channel effects, collisions, interference from other systems and nodes coming and going. In the 2.4 GHz ISM band, heavily loaded WLAN hot-spots can cause a high packet error rate.
sections.eli5: Picture thousands of little walkie-talkies on lampposts and houses, running on small batteries. Some listen, some do jobs like switching lights, and a few are helpers that pass messages along or link to the Internet.

sections.title: Use Cases and Traffic Patterns
sections.content:
The RFC walks through five scenarios. In deployment, nodes arrive in batches and the network must start up, with address allocation, roles and schedules. If nodes are initialized before roll-out they all hear each other, and pre-programmed MAC and routing protocols may waste a lot of energy. After roll-out nodes typically have about 5 to 10 one-hop neighbors, though some have hundreds. When nodes join or disappear, for example from a depleted battery or theft, the protocol should convey that so the network can reconfigure.

Regular reporting is usually low frequency, in the range of once per hour or per day, so end-to-end latency and acknowledgements are not vital. Queried reporting happens at random times, with latencies of seconds or minutes being fine. Alert reporting is rare, such as toxic gas above a threshold or a full recycling glass container, and deliveries within seconds should suffice in most cases.

The information flow is highly directional: sensed data goes from sensors through LBRs to applications outside the network, queries go from outside through LBRs to sensors, and control information goes to actuators. Sensed data is likely to be correlated in space and time. The network should handle bursts such as a city-wide power outage, where devices run on a temporary "last gasp" source and a node must send its own alert while still forwarding others' traffic.
sections.eli5: Most of the time the sensors whisper a number once an hour. Now and then someone asks a question, and once in a while an alarm has to get through fast.

sections.title: The Routing Requirements
sections.content:
Section 6 states the requirements using RFC 2119 words. The main ones:

  • Scalability: the protocol MUST organize a large number of sensing nodes into regions of the order of 10^2 to 10^4 nodes each, and MUST scale to very many nodes without performance dropping below configurable thresholds.
  • Parameter-constrained routing: the protocol MUST be able to advertise node capabilities, such as CPU, memory and battery level, for use in routing decisions. Nodes SHOULD compute and install different paths to the same destination depending on the traffic, possibly using IPv6 marking such as DSCP or Flow Label.
  • Autonomous and alien configuration: the protocol MUST provide zero-configuration at ramp-up, self-organization after topology changes, and support for externally supplied patches and configuration updates, using multicast and anycast.
  • Highly directed flows: the protocol MUST handle traffic bursts by computing and selecting multiple paths to the same destination. Traffic concentrates near the LBR, which can unbalance node load.
  • Multicast and anycast: the protocol MUST support unicast, multicast and anycast.
  • Network dynamicity: local changes SHOULD NOT force the whole network to reorganize, and convergence and route establishment times SHOULD be significantly lower than the smallest reporting interval.
  • Latency: except for alerts, the network is delay tolerant if data arrives within a fraction of the smallest reporting interval. The protocol SHOULD support routing by different metrics, one of which could be latency.
sections.eli5: The rules say the routing must work with huge numbers of nodes, care about who is low on battery, set itself up with no human, fix small breaks locally and still get urgent messages through quickly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Wireless, distributed networks have many routing security threats, and resource-limited nodes cannot run heavy security. A routing security approach SHOULD be lightweight enough to run on all nodes. The U-LLN MUST deny any node that has not been authenticated and authorized to take part in routing decisions, and routing protocols MUST support message integrity. Protocols proposed for U-LLNs MUST support authentication and integrity measures and SHOULD support confidentiality.

Self-configuration adds risk: a node MUST authenticate to a trusted, already associated node before joining self-configuration, and associated nodes MUST deny resources to unauthenticated peers. The protocol SHOULD defend against denial of service, such as forwarding loops or excess overhead traffic. Damage SHOULD be commensurate with the number of nodes physically compromised, so one captured node SHOULD NOT deny service to the whole network. The U-LLN SHOULD NOT interface with an external network, such as a home network, that has not established trust.
sections.eli5: Only trusted helpers may join the message-passing game, and one bad helper must not be able to wreck the whole game.

items.title: Scalability
items.text: Regions of about 10^2 to 10^4 sensing nodes each.

items.title: Parameter-constrained routing
items.text: Advertise CPU, memory and battery capabilities for routing decisions.

items.title: Autonomous configuration
items.text: Zero-configuration at ramp-up and self-organization after changes.

items.title: Directed flows
items.text: Many nodes report to few LBRs; use multiple paths for bursts.

items.title: Unicast, multicast, anycast
items.text: All three transmission schemes must be supported.

items.title: Network dynamicity
items.text: Local changes should not reorganize the whole network.

items.title: Latency
items.text: Tolerant except for alerts; route by different metrics.
